project: Rosnet Case Study — URL Health Monitor
about: Decision log for defending choices in the Rosnet panel. Each decision lists alternatives, tradeoffs, a plain (STE-100) explanation, and how AI was involved. Edge cases are logged here and fixed only at the end, by priority.

timebox.notes: Clock starts with the first line of application code. Planning and setup before that are logged separately below.

decisions.title: C# with ASP.NET Core 10 Minimal APIs
decisions.decision: Build the backend in C# on ASP.NET Core 10 (current LTS) using Minimal APIs.

alternatives.whyNot: My strongest language, but Rosnet is a .NET shop and the brief encourages C#/ASP.NET Core.
More files and ceremony for about five endpoints.

decisions.rationale: Matches Rosnet's stack. Minimal APIs keep each endpoint to a few lines, close to Express route handlers.
decisions.tradeoffs: I am newer to C#, so I must learn and explain backend concepts as I go (tracked in docs/CONCEPTS.md).
decisions.plain: The server is written in C#. Rosnet uses C#. Minimal APIs let us write each web address handler in a few lines, like Express.

ai.accepted: Minimal APIs

decisions.title: React 18 + Vite, no frameworks
decisions.decision: React 18 built with Vite. Plain CSS and native fetch. No Next.js, Tailwind, UI kits, or chart libraries.

alternatives.whyNot: Server rendering and routing are not needed for one dashboard page. Heavier.
Deprecated.
No JSX without a build step; awkward to work with.

decisions.rationale: Vite is a build tool, not a framework. It gives JSX and a fast dev server with very few dependencies.
decisions.tradeoffs: The Vite React template now installs React 19, so React 18 must be pinned on purpose.
decisions.plain: Vite turns our React files into files a browser can read. It does not add rules about how to build the app.

ai.suggestedBy: me (React 18, no frameworks), Claude (Vite, pin React 18)
ai.accepted: all

decisions.title: Plain JavaScript instead of TypeScript
decisions.decision: Write the frontend in plain JavaScript. Optional JSDoc comments on API helpers for editor hints.

alternatives.whyNot: Costs time inside a 3-hour cap. Its main win here is typing a handful of fetch calls.

decisions.rationale: I can write and defend plain JavaScript fastest. The C# backend is already strongly typed; the only untyped edge is a few API calls.
decisions.tradeoffs: No compile-time check that the frontend matches the API shape. Next step: add TypeScript and generate the client from the OpenAPI spec.
decisions.plain: We write the screen code in plain JavaScript. It is faster for me. We can add TypeScript later.

ai.rejected: TypeScript — I overruled it for time and ownership; Claude agreed on review.

decisions.title: SQLite instead of Postgres
decisions.decision: Store URLs, settings, and check results in a single SQLite file.

alternatives.whyNot: Reviewers would need Docker or a local install before running the app.
History must survive a restart.

decisions.rationale: Zero setup for the panel: clone and run. One process writes small rows on a schedule, which fits SQLite well.
decisions.tradeoffs: SQLite allows one writer at a time and is not shared across servers. Production path: Postgres, with time-based partitioning or TimescaleDB for history.
decisions.plain: SQLite keeps all data in one file. Nothing extra is needed to run it. A big real system would use Postgres.

ai.accepted: SQLite

decisions.title: Dapper instead of EF Core
decisions.decision: Use Dapper over Microsoft.Data.Sqlite with hand-written SQL. Create tables with one SQL script at startup.

alternatives.whyNot: Heavier, generates SQL I would need to explain, migrations add setup. Like Prisma: more hidden behavior.
No extra package, but much more boilerplate to map rows to objects.

decisions.rationale: Two small packages. Every query is visible SQL I can read and defend, like using 'pg' or 'better-sqlite3' in Node.
decisions.tradeoffs: No migrations; schema changes are manual. Fine for a take-home, not for a long-lived product.
decisions.plain: Dapper runs SQL that we write. It turns each row into a C# object. We can read every query.

ai.accepted: Dapper

decisions.title: Scheduler: BackgroundService + PeriodicTimer, no job library
decisions.decision: One BackgroundService ticks on a PeriodicTimer, finds URLs that are due (per-URL interval), and checks them in parallel with a concurrency cap and a per-request timeout via IHttpClientFactory.

alternatives.whyNot: Extra dependency and storage tables for a single recurring job.
More moving parts to start, stop, and update when intervals change.

decisions.rationale: Built into .NET. A single 'what is due now?' loop makes per-URL intervals simple and interval changes take effect on the next tick.
decisions.tradeoffs: Runs in one process only; two app instances would double-check. Fine for this scope.
decisions.plain: A loop wakes up every few seconds. It finds the web addresses that need a check now. It checks them at the same time, but not too many at once.

ai.accepted: pending build

decisions.title: One process serves the API and the built UI
decisions.decision: ASP.NET Core serves the built React app from wwwroot. In development, Vite proxies /api to the backend.

alternatives.whyNot: Reviewers would need to start two things and deal with CORS.

decisions.rationale: One command to run the demo, no CORS setup.
decisions.tradeoffs: Frontend must be built before running the backend in 'production' mode.
decisions.plain: One program sends both the data and the web page. You start one thing.

ai.accepted: pending build

decisions.title: Configurable intervals: per-URL check interval, history window, retention
decisions.decision: In scope: each URL has its own check interval; the UI picks a history time window; a global retention period deletes old results.

alternatives.whyNot: Simpler, but I want the UI to configure checks per URL.

decisions.rationale: Per-URL intervals fall out of the 'what is due now?' scheduler (D-006) at low cost. Retention is one DELETE query on a timer. History window is a query parameter.
decisions.tradeoffs: Per-URL intervals are listed as bonus scope in the brief and add risk to the 3-hour cap. Claude flagged this; I kept it.
decisions.plain: You can set how often each web address is checked. You can pick how far back to look. Old results are deleted after a set time.

decisions.title: Test core requirements only; log edge cases for the end
decisions.decision: xUnit tests cover only core behavior: a check records status, response time and healthy/unhealthy (including unreachable = unhealthy); results persist; history reads back. Edge cases are logged in edgeCases and fixed at the end by priority if time allows.

alternatives.whyNot: Does not fit 3 hours; the brief warns against shallow tests piled up for a number.

decisions.rationale: The brief asks what was tested, what was skipped, and why. A ranked edge-case list answers that directly.
decisions.tradeoffs: Known gaps exist on purpose and are documented.
decisions.plain: We test the main jobs first. We write down the rare problems. We fix them at the end if there is time.

decisions.title: Light dependencies, visible AI use, decision log in the repo
decisions.decision: Ask before adding any package. Commit log.json and docs/CONCEPTS.md. Keep Co-Authored-By: Claude on AI-assisted commits. Use GSD (open-gsd/gsd-core) for planning.

alternatives.whyNot: The panel explicitly asks how AI was used and what was thrown out; the log is the evidence.

decisions.rationale: Shows the decision process and honest AI use, which the brief says it will dig into.
decisions.tradeoffs: The panel sees my learning notes for backend concepts. That is intentional.
decisions.plain: We keep few add-on packages. We show where AI helped. We save our reasons in the project.

ai.accepted: all

decisions.title: Context management: fresh session per GSD step instead of /compact
decisions.decision: Run each GSD step (discuss, plan, execute, verify) in a new session. State lives on disk in .planning/, log.json and docs/CONCEPTS.md. Use /gsd-pause-work and /gsd-resume-work for mid-phase stops.

alternatives.whyNot: Each summary loses detail; decisions and reasoning drift over time.
Could not be verified in this setup; GSD already provides phase-sized steps with on-disk state.
Runs all phases without stopping; I need to make and understand each decision to defend it.

decisions.rationale: Fresh sessions start with a clean context and read only the files they need. Execution already runs in subagents with their own context.
decisions.tradeoffs: Each new session spends a little time re-reading state files.
decisions.plain: We start a new chat for each step. The plan and notes are saved in files. The new chat reads the files and continues.

ai.accepted: GSD phase loop

decisions.title: Four extras in v1 as a stretch tier, built last
decisions.decision: Pause/resume, check now, URL detail view, and response-time sparkline are v1 but built after all core requirements, in that order, and cut from the bottom if the 3-hour cap is reached. Deferred edge cases (EDGE-01) come after the extras.

alternatives.whyNot: Risks a half-done core if time runs out.
Each is cheap and shows UX judgment; worth attempting once the core is safe.

decisions.rationale: Core value is protected first. Order is cost-to-value: pause/resume and check now are small backend additions; the detail view adds a screen; the sparkline is polish.
decisions.tradeoffs: Total scope is large for 3 hours. Whatever is cut gets listed in the README as next steps.
decisions.plain: We build the main parts first. Then we add the extra parts, one at a time. If time ends, we stop and write down what is left.

ai.accepted: all

decisions.title: Turn off GSD UI safety gate; vertical MVP roadmap approved
decisions.decision: Approved a 5-phase vertical-MVP roadmap (3 core phases, 2 stretch). Turned off workflow.ui_safety_gate so UI phases do not need a separate design spec before planning.

alternatives.option: Keep the gate on (UI-SPEC for Phases 1-4)
alternatives.whyNot: Four extra design steps; the brief says a working app with a clear README beats a pretty UI.

alternatives.option: Horizontal layers (DB, then API, then UI)
alternatives.whyNot: Nothing works end to end until the end; risky under a 3-hour cap.

decisions.rationale: Each phase ends with a working app. The README lands in Phase 3, so the submission is complete even if stretch phases are cut.
decisions.tradeoffs: No up-front UI design contract; layout decisions are made during planning, with plain CSS.
decisions.plain: Each step gives us an app that works. We skip the extra design step because the task does not ask for a pretty screen.

ai.suggestedBy: Claude (roadmapper agent flagged the gate; Claude recommended turning it off)
ai.accepted: all

decisions.title: Phase 1 defaults: repo layout, data model, API, seeds, check behavior, dashboard
decisions.decision: server/ + web/ + tests/ with one solution file. Vite builds into server/wwwroot (gitignored); an MSBuild target runs npm install/build when missing so a fresh-clone dotnet run works. Tables: urls(id, url, interval_seconds, created_at) and check_results(id, url_id, checked_at, status_code?, response_time_ms, healthy, error?), ISO UTC text times, last-checked derived from newest result. GET /api/urls returns each URL with its lastCheck or null. Seeds: example.com, github.com, a GitHub 404 page, unreachable.invalid. 5s tick, 10s timeout, GET with ResponseHeadersRead, follow redirects, sequential checks in Phase 1. Plain table with dot + word status. Tick (5s) and timeout (10s) are defaults in appsettings.json: operator config, not UI settings.

alternatives.option: Commit the built UI into wwwroot
alternatives.whyNot: Noisy diffs and the UI can go stale.

alternatives.option: Manual npm build step before dotnet run
alternatives.whyNot: Breaks the one-command promise (D-007).

alternatives.option: Store last_checked_at on the urls row
alternatives.whyNot: Two places to keep in sync; the newest result already has it.
Some servers answer 405 to HEAD, which would show a false unhealthy.

alternatives.option: httpstat.us or httpbin as the failing seed
alternatives.whyNot: Third-party test services are often down; .invalid can never resolve.

alternatives.option: Make tick and timeout editable in the UI
alternatives.whyNot: No requirement asks for it; adds a form, a settings column, and validation inside the 3-hour cap. Per-URL timeout is a README next step.

decisions.rationale: Smallest version that meets the Phase 1 success criteria and keeps every piece easy to explain.
decisions.tradeoffs: Owner did not weigh these one by one; any can be changed before planning. Fresh-clone build needs Node installed. No migrations, so schema changes mean deleting the local DB file.
decisions.plain: The server code, the screen code, and the tests each get a folder. Starting the server also builds the screen the first time. We keep each check as its own row. The screen shows one table row per web address.

ai.accepted: all — owner skipped the discussion step and said build it
ai.changed: Owner asked whether tick and timeout were UI-configurable; agreed to move them from hard-coded values to appsettings.json.

decisions.title: Cut GSD process overhead to protect the 3-hour cap
decisions.decision: Merge old Phases 2 (Health Over Time) and 3 (URL Management, Retention & README) into one Phase 2 "Features & README", run as /gsd-quick tasks. Old Phases 4 (extras) and 5 (edge cases) are no longer phases: they become /gsd-quick tasks done only if time remains. In .planning/config.json, turn off plan_check, discuss (skip_discuss), pattern_mapper, ui_phase, ai_integration_phase, api_coverage_gate, assumption_delta, specless_probe_fallback, security_enforcement, and post_planning_gaps. Code review and the goal verifier stay on for Phase 1 only, then go off.

alternatives.option: Keep the full discuss → plan → check → execute → verify loop for all 5 phases
alternatives.whyNot: The ceremony alone could use up most of the 3-hour cap; about an hour went to process before any code.
Mixes core work with stretch work, so the plan gets bigger and it is less clear where to stop.

alternatives.option: Keep 5 phases but run each as /gsd-quick
alternatives.whyNot: Keeps phase bookkeeping for phases that may be cut anyway.

alternatives.option: Turn code review and verifier off now
alternatives.whyNot: Phase 1 sets up the base that everything else builds on, so one check there is worth the time.

decisions.rationale: The phases left are small and the stack and decisions are locked, so the extra planning gates add time but little value. CLAUDE.md already says to log edge cases rather than build them, so the edge-case probe and the threat model repeat that rule.
decisions.tradeoffs: Fewer automatic checks on plans for Phase 2 and later, so mistakes are found by running the app and the core tests instead. The Phase 1 plan was already started with the old settings, so it still has a threat model and edge-case items.
decisions.plain: The planning tool was doing many extra checks. They took more time than the code. We turned most of them off. We joined the last steps into one. Extra features happen only if time is left.

ai.suggestedBy: Claude listed the overhead sources; owner asked to apply them
ai.accepted: All of it: merge 2+3, drop 4+5 as phases, gates off, review and verifier for Phase 1 only (both picked from Claude's recommended options).

decisions.title: Phase 1 dependency set (exact packages and versions)
decisions.decision: Server: NuGet Microsoft.Data.Sqlite 10.0.14 and Dapper 2.1.89. Web: react ^18.3.1 and react-dom ^18.3.1 as dependencies; vite ^8.3.6 and @vitejs/plugin-react ^6.2.1 as devDependencies. Nothing else. web/package.json was written by hand. plugin-react's optional peers (@rolldown/plugin-babel, babel-plugin-react-compiler, oxc-transform-react) were left uninstalled.

alternatives.whyNot: It defaults to React 19 and adds ESLint and other extras we did not approve. We would have to remove them by hand.

alternatives.option: Install plugin-react's optional peers (React Compiler, Babel)
alternatives.whyNot: We do not use them. Each one is another package to explain to the panel.

decisions.rationale: These are exactly the packages approved under D-002, D-004 and D-005. Fewer packages means fewer lines the owner must defend.
decisions.tradeoffs: A hand-written package.json has no lint script or editor defaults. That is fine for a small plain-JavaScript app. Version ranges are caret ranges, so package-lock.json is what pins the real versions.
decisions.plain: We added only the packages we had already agreed on. We wrote the web package file by hand. The Vite starter adds React 19 and extra tools. We did not want those.

ai.accepted: The package set and hand-written scaffold, as planned. The owner approved the packages earlier in D-002, D-004 and D-005 and accepted the Phase 1 defaults in D-014.

decisions.title: Local address: http://localhost:5080, http only, browser stays closed
decisions.decision: The server listens on http://localhost:5080. The launch profile is http only (the https profile was deleted) and launchBrowser is false.

alternatives.whyNot: macOS AirPlay Receiver uses port 5000, so the app can fail to start on a Mac.
The panel would have to trust a local development certificate before the app runs.

decisions.rationale: This is a local demo with no login and no private data, so https adds setup but no safety. The panel only needs to open one address.
decisions.tradeoffs: Traffic is not encrypted. That is acceptable on localhost. A real deployment would sit behind https. The README must say to open the address by hand.
decisions.plain: The app runs at one local address. It uses http, not https. This way nobody has to trust a certificate. The browser does not open by itself.

ai.accepted: Port 5080, http only, no auto-open, as planned. The owner accepted the Phase 1 defaults in D-014.

decisions.title: History window API: ?window=1h|24h|7d with a summary and the 30 newest checks per URL
decisions.decision: GET /api/urls?window=1h|24h|7d returns the Phase 1 fields plus summary {checkCount, uptimePercent, avgResponseTimeMs, recent}. recent is the 30 newest checks inside the window, oldest first. The server works out each summary with two small SQL queries per URL (one COUNT/AVG, one ORDER BY checked_at DESC LIMIT 30). GET /api/urls/{id}/checks?window= returns every check of one URL inside the window (HIST-03). The window is a fixed whitelist: no window means 1h, any other value returns 400. The cutoff is DateTime.UtcNow minus the window, passed to SQL as ISO 'o' UTC text. The dashboard polls every 5 seconds.

alternatives.option: Send every check to the browser and compute in JavaScript
alternatives.whyNot: A 7d window holds about 20,000 checks per 30s URL. The browser would download them all on every poll.

alternatives.option: One GROUP BY for the stats plus a ROW_NUMBER() window-function query for the strip
alternatives.whyNot: Fewer queries, but it adds another SQL concept and a merge by url_id in C#. It still numbers every row in the window.
Two requests per poll and merge code in JavaScript.

alternatives.option: A strip of time buckets that covers the whole window
alternatives.whyNot: ROADMAP Phase 2 criterion 2 says each check is colored. Buckets also need more SQL date math. Good for README Next steps.
Right at scale, but too much for the 3-hour cap.

decisions.rationale: One request per poll, with a size that does not depend on the window. Each summary query uses the existing (url_id, checked_at) index. The window filter sits in Database methods that take the cutoff as a parameter, so a test can call them directly.
decisions.tradeoffs: 1 + 2N queries per poll. That is fine for a handful of URLs in an in-process database. The aggregate still reads every row in the window every 5 seconds: a 7d window is about 20,000 rows per 30s URL, and a rollup table is the next step. The strip shows only the newest 30 checks. In a fresh demo with less than 1 hour of data, the three windows look the same, so the README must say this.
decisions.plain: The browser asks for one window: 1 hour, 1 day, or 7 days. The server counts the checks inside that window and sends the totals. It also sends the 30 newest checks for the colored boxes. The browser never gets thousands of rows. The page asks again every 5 seconds.

ai.suggestedBy: Claude (orchestrator steer, then Claude as planner)
ai.accepted: The window query parameter, the summary and recent shape, the 400 for unknown windows, and 5 second polling.
ai.changed: The orchestrator steer suggested one GROUP BY for all URLs. The planner changed it to one small query per URL, because the strip needs a per-URL LIMIT query anyway.
ai.rejected: Sending all checks to the browser, a separate stats endpoint, time buckets, and a rollup table. The owner has not yet reviewed this decision in a session: read it before the panel.

decisions.title: Average response time counts only checks that got an HTTP response
decisions.decision: avgResponseTimeMs averages response_time_ms only for checks where status_code is not NULL (a 2xx to 5xx answer). The SQL uses AVG over CASE WHEN status_code IS NOT NULL, and AVG skips NULL.

alternatives.whyNot: A DNS failure adds about 2 ms and a timeout adds 10,000 ms. Neither is a response time, so 'how fast it answers' gets mixed with 'how fast it fails'.
The 404 seed answers, but it would show a dash instead of its real time.

decisions.rationale: A response time only means something when the server answered. Uptime % already shows the failures.
decisions.tradeoffs: A URL that often times out can still show a good average. Uptime % is the stat that shows those failures.
decisions.plain: The average time counts only the checks where the website answered. A failed lookup or a timeout is not an answer, so it stays out of the average. The uptime number still shows those failures.

ai.accepted: Average only checks that got an HTTP response.
ai.rejected: Averaging every check, and averaging only healthy checks. This was not in the orchestrator steer.

decisions.title: Core tests: xUnit with a fake HttpMessageHandler and temp SQLite files
decisions.decision: One test project (tests/HealthMonitor.Tests) with exactly three packages: xunit 2.9.3, xunit.runner.visualstudio 4.0.1, Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk 18.11.0. UrlChecker is tested with a hand-written fake HttpMessageHandler (no network). Database is tested against a new temp SQLite file per test. 12 tests: status classification incl. the 399/400 boundary, measured response time, unreachable, timeout (CHK-02..04); save + read back after a new Database object (HIST-01/02); window read-back (HIST-03); uptime/average summary (DASH-03). Each test was shown to fail by breaking the code it guards (<= 399 -> < 399; window filter disabled).

alternatives.option: Moq or NSubstitute for the HTTP layer
alternatives.whyNot: An extra package to explain; a 5-line fake handler does the same.
Each new connection gets an empty DB, so the restart test could not reuse it; a temp file mirrors the real app.
Needs Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing and starts the background scheduler; the core logic is already covered by calling the classes directly.
Slow and flaky; a site being down would fail the build for the wrong reason.

decisions.rationale: Smallest setup that covers the core requirements and can fail for a real reason (CLAUDE.md section 5).
decisions.tradeoffs: The HTTP endpoints, the scheduler loop, and the React UI have no automated tests; they were checked by running the app. Edge cases have no tests by design (D-009).
decisions.plain: We test the two most important parts. One part checks a web address. The other part saves and reads results. A fake server gives fixed answers, so the tests do not need the internet. Each test uses its own new database file.

ai.accepted: Owner approved the three packages and building the tests inline in the session (no planner run).

decisions.title: URL management: POST, PATCH and DELETE on /api/urls
decisions.decision: POST /api/urls {url, intervalSeconds} -> 201 {id}; PATCH /api/urls/{id} {intervalSeconds} -> 204 or 404; DELETE /api/urls/{id} -> 204 or 404, deleting the URL and its history in one transaction. No server-side validation yet (EC-002, EC-003, EC-004 stay deferred); the form uses type=url and min=10 in the browser only. The UI reloads at once after a change by bumping a version counter that re-runs the polling effect.

alternatives.option: PUT /api/urls/{id} with the whole URL object
alternatives.whyNot: Only the interval can change, so PATCH with one field is the honest shape.

alternatives.option: Keep history when a URL is removed (soft delete)
alternatives.whyNot: Adds an 'active' flag to every query; the brief asks to remove URLs. Pause/resume (EXTRA-01) is the place for keeping history.

alternatives.option: Validate URL and interval on the server now
alternatives.whyNot: CLAUDE.md section 4: edge cases are logged first and fixed at the end in priority order.

decisions.rationale: Smallest set of endpoints that meets URL-01..03, using the HTTP verbs a reviewer expects.
decisions.tradeoffs: Bad input can be saved through the API (the browser form blocks the obvious cases). Remove is permanent and also deletes history, so the UI asks for confirmation.
decisions.plain: Three new server calls let the page add a web address, change how often it is checked, or remove it. Removing it also removes its old results.

ai.accepted: Built inline in the session after the owner said yes to task 3.

decisions.status: amended by D-023 (DELETE is now a soft delete)

decisions.title: Concurrent checks: start without awaiting, SemaphoreSlim cap, in-flight set
decisions.decision: Each tick, the scheduler starts every due check as its own task and does not wait for it. A SemaphoreSlim (Monitor:MaxConcurrentChecks = 4 in appsettings.json) limits how many run at once; extra checks wait for a free slot. A ConcurrentDictionary of URL ids in flight stops a slow URL from being started again on the next tick. Each task logs its own errors because nobody awaits it.

alternatives.option: Parallel.ForEachAsync over the due URLs, awaited per tick
alternatives.whyNot: Shorter, but a URL that takes the full 10 s timeout still holds the whole pass, so every other URL's next check waits up to 10 s. CHK-05 says one slow URL must not delay the others.
Many timers to create, change and dispose when URLs are added, re-timed or removed; the single loop already handles all three by reading the DB each tick.
More moving parts than a semaphore for the same result at this size.

decisions.rationale: Meets CHK-05 strictly. Shown with a local socket that never answers: example.org was saved 9 s before the hanging URL timed out.
decisions.tradeoffs: Fire-and-forget tasks are harder to follow than an awaited loop, and a check can finish after its URL is deleted (EC-023). The cap is global, not per host.
decisions.plain: The checker now checks up to 4 web addresses at the same time. It does not wait for a slow one before it starts the others. It also never checks the same address twice at once.

ai.accepted: Owner approved task 3; Claude picked the non-awaited design over Parallel.ForEachAsync after reasoning that an awaited pass still blocks the next tick for up to 10 s.

decisions.title: No hard deletes: soft-delete URLs, archive old results, show everything on an All-checks page
decisions.decision: Owner rule: never hard-delete data. (1) Removing a URL sets urls.deleted_at; the scheduler and dashboard skip it, its results stay. (2) Retention (CONF-01/02) keeps its UI setting and timer, but a RetentionSweeper moves results older than retention_days (settings table, default 30) from check_results into check_results_archive in one transaction instead of deleting them. (3) A new All-checks page (#/checks) lists every result, live and archived, removed URLs included, marked as such. Existing DBs get the deleted_at column via a one-time ALTER at startup.

alternatives.option: Hard delete as the brief words it ('Results older than it are deleted on a timer')
alternatives.whyNot: Owner wants full history preserved; archiving still removes old rows from the live table, which is the practical point of retention (small, fast window queries).
The live table keeps growing and every query must remember the filter; a separate table keeps the dashboard queries unchanged.

alternatives.option: Keep the hard DELETE for URLs from D-021
alternatives.whyNot: Contradicts the no-hard-delete rule and loses history on one click.

decisions.rationale: Meets the owner's no-data-loss rule and the brief's retention requirement in spirit: old results leave the live table on a timer, controlled by a UI setting.
decisions.tradeoffs: Deviates from the brief's literal wording ('deleted'); the README must say so. Storage grows without limit (EC-026). Removed URLs cannot be restored yet (EC-027).
decisions.plain: We never throw data away. Old results move to a second table. Removed web addresses are only hidden. A history page shows everything.

ai.suggestedBy: Owner set the no-hard-delete rule; Claude flagged that it conflicts with the brief's retention wording and offered three options
ai.accepted: Owner chose 'archive, don't delete' and soft delete for URL rows.
ai.rejected: Hard delete; soft-delete flag on results

decisions.title: Sorting and paging: SQL for All checks, C# for the dashboard, fixed lists of sort keys
decisions.decision: Both GET /api/urls and GET /api/checks take sort, dir (asc|desc), page (>=1), pageSize (10|50|100) and return {total, rows}; anything else is 400. All checks sorts and pages in SQL (ORDER BY + LIMIT/OFFSET over a UNION ALL of live and archive). The dashboard sorts and pages in C# after building its rows, because uptime/average are computed per URL and the list is one row per URL. Sort keys map to fixed column expressions in a dictionary, so client text never reaches the SQL string. The UI switches views with the URL hash instead of a router package. Column widths/row heights use CSS resize (stretch).

alternatives.option: Sort the dashboard in SQL too
alternatives.whyNot: Uptime and average come from a per-URL query; doing it in SQL would need one large GROUP BY rewrite for a list of 4–10 rows.
Owner asked for FE and BE sorting, and All checks can hold thousands of rows.
Better for a growing table (EC-028) but harder to explain and to combine with arbitrary sort columns in the time left.
New package for two views; a hash check is 10 lines.

decisions.rationale: Smallest design that gives real server-side sorting and paging where the data is large, without SQL injection risk.
decisions.tradeoffs: The dashboard still loads every URL's summary before paging (fine at this size). OFFSET paging can shift rows (EC-028). Resized widths are not saved (EC-029).
decisions.plain: You can click a column title to sort, and pick 10, 50, or 100 rows per page. The server does the sorting. It only accepts column names from a fixed list, so nobody can sneak in database commands.

ai.suggestedBy: Owner asked for sorting (FE and BE), 10/50/100 paging, colors, and resizable columns/rows; Claude chose where each sort runs
ai.accepted: Owner chose sorting/paging on both tables over the recommended All-checks-only option.

decisions.title: Row actions: play/pause, trash icon, per-URL history modal; inline SVG icons and native <dialog>
decisions.decision: Every column gets a play/pause toggle (PATCH {paused}); urls.paused_at marks a paused URL, the scheduler skips it, and the row says 'Paused' (EXTRA-01). No separate 'stop': the trash can (soft delete, D-023) already stops monitoring for good. The Recent checks cell gets a history button that opens a native <dialog> with every check for that URL, live and archived, reusing the All-checks table with ?urlId= (EXTRA-03). Icons (plus, trash, play, pause, history) are hand-written inline SVG. Sort arrows always show (↕ when unsorted). The row-height handle sits in the Status column; the URL input is larger. Amended same day by the owner: play/pause moved to the Actions column next to the trash can; all icons dark green; the 'Stored in' (live/archive) column was removed from the history tables, so archived rows are no longer labeled in the UI (the API still returns archived).

alternatives.option: Play / pause / stop with 'stop' as a third state
alternatives.whyNot: Stop would duplicate either pause or the trash can; owner chose play + pause only.
A new dependency for five icons; inline SVG is a few lines each.

alternatives.option: A custom modal with a fixed overlay div
alternatives.whyNot: <dialog>.showModal() gives Escape to close, a backdrop, and focus trapping without extra code.

alternatives.option: History modal limited to the selected window
alternatives.whyNot: Owner wanted the entire history; the window already drives the stats and strip.

decisions.rationale: Owner-requested UI refinements, built with no new packages and reusing existing endpoints and components.
decisions.tradeoffs: Paused URLs still count in the dashboard's sort and paging. The modal is not polled; it has a Refresh button.
decisions.plain: Each row now has a play and pause button, a trash can, and a clock button. The clock button opens a window with every check for that web address.

ai.suggestedBy: Owner listed the UI changes; Claude asked what 'stop' should mean and what the modal should show
ai.accepted: Play + pause only; modal shows the URL's full history, paged

decisions.title: Server-side input rules in one static class (EC-002, EC-003)
decisions.decision: InputRules.cs holds two pure functions that return an error message or null: IntervalProblem (10..86400 s) and UrlProblem (absolute http/https URL; not localhost, *.local, or a loopback/private/link-local/unique-local IP literal). POST and PATCH /api/urls return 400 {error} on a problem; api.js shows that message in the UI.

alternatives.whyNot: Attributes need extra wiring in Minimal APIs, and FluentValidation is a new package; two small functions are easier to read and defend.

alternatives.option: Resolve DNS and block private results now
alternatives.whyNot: Correct only if done at connect time (DNS can change); that is a custom ConnectCallback, logged as EC-031.

alternatives.option: Keep relying on the form's min/type=url
alternatives.whyNot: The API is reachable directly, so the browser's checks protect nothing.

decisions.rationale: Fixes the two priority-1 edge cases with the smallest code and makes the SSRF risk visible in one place.
decisions.tradeoffs: Literal-address SSRF only (EC-031). The 1-day maximum is a judgment call.
decisions.plain: The server now checks what you type before saving it. It refuses addresses that are not real web addresses, addresses inside our own network, and check times that are too fast or too slow.

ai.suggestedBy: Claude (priority-1 edge cases after the core was done)
ai.accepted: Owner said yes to fixing priority-1 edge cases.

decisions.title: More tests at the owner's request: input rules, soft delete, pause, duplicates, paging, and frontend logic with node:test
decisions.decision: Backend: 24 new xUnit cases (InputRulesTests; DatabaseTests for soft delete keeping history, pause flag, duplicate rule, All-checks paging) -> 37 total. Frontend: UI decision logic (nextSort, sortArrow, pageCount, rowStatus, formatPercent/formatMs, checkTooltip) moved from components into web/src/logic.js and tested with Node's built-in test runner (web/src/logic.test.js, 7 tests, `npm --prefix web test`). Component rendering is not tested.

alternatives.whyNot: Three or more new packages, and CLAUDE.md requires asking first; the 10-minute budget did not allow that conversation. node:test covers the logic with zero packages.
Owner asked to add any relevant tests that were missed; the SSRF guard and soft delete are behavior the panel will ask about.

decisions.rationale: Covers the behavior added after the first test pass, including the security rule, without new dependencies.
decisions.tradeoffs: Relaxes D-009 (no edge-case tests): InputRules tests cover fixed edge cases. No component/DOM tests; layout was checked by screenshots instead.
decisions.plain: We added tests for the new rules and for the screen's logic. The screen tests use a tool that comes with Node, so we did not add any packages.

ai.suggestedBy: Owner asked for frontend unit tests and any missed tests; Claude chose node:test to avoid unapproved packages
ai.accepted: Built within the owner's 10-minute window.

decisions.title: Check now: POST /api/urls/{id}/check runs one check in the request
decisions.decision: The endpoint runs UrlChecker with the same named HttpClient (same timeout and User-Agent), saves the result with InsertCheckResultAsync, and returns it. It works on paused URLs (a manual request) and returns 404 for removed ones. The UI button is disabled until the request finishes.

alternatives.option: Queue the check in the scheduler (e.g. clear the URL's due time)
alternatives.whyNot: The scheduler would need to be shared as a singleton and the user would wait up to one tick; doing it in the request is simpler and gives the result back directly.

decisions.rationale: Smallest code that meets EXTRA-02 and reuses the checker and insert exactly as the scheduler does.
decisions.tradeoffs: The scheduler's in-flight set does not see manual checks, so a manual check and a scheduled one for the same URL can overlap once; both are saved as separate rows. The request can take up to the 10 s timeout.
decisions.plain: A lightning button checks one web address right away and saves the result like any other check.

ai.suggestedBy: Claude (next item on the stretch list)
ai.accepted: Owner said proceed.

decisions.title: Sparkline: inline SVG over the strip's recent checks, inside the Recent checks cell
decisions.decision: sparklinePoints() in logic.js maps the window's 30 newest checks (the same data as the strip) to polyline points, skipping no-response checks. The SVG sits above the strip in the same cell, so no new column is needed at 1280 px.

alternatives.option: Plot every check in the window
alternatives.whyNot: A 7d window is ~20k points per URL on every 5 s poll (the reason for D-018); 30 points show the trend.
Banned by the stack rules and unnecessary for one polyline.
Would push the table past 1280 px again.

decisions.rationale: Meets EXTRA-04 with no new data, no package, and a tested pure function.
decisions.tradeoffs: The line covers the newest 30 checks in the window, not the whole window; the scale is per row, so heights are not comparable across rows.
decisions.plain: A small line above the colored boxes shows if a web address is getting faster or slower.

ai.accepted: Owner said proceed.
ai.rejected: The sparkline itself: owner removed it after seeing it, because the moving line was too much visual noise.

edgeCases.title: Overlapping checks for the same URL
edgeCases.description: A slow check (near the timeout) is still running when the URL is due again, so two checks run at once.
edgeCases.plain: A check can take a long time. The next check can start before the first one ends.
edgeCases.fixedNote: Phase 2 task 3: an in-flight set in CheckScheduler skips a URL whose check is still running (D-022).

edgeCases.title: Very short intervals
edgeCases.description: A 1-second interval would hammer the target and flood the database. Needs a minimum.
edgeCases.plain: If you check too often, you send too much traffic. We need a smallest allowed time.
edgeCases.fixedNote: InputRules.IntervalProblem: POST and PATCH refuse intervals outside 10 s..86400 s with a 400 and a reason.

edgeCases.title: Invalid URL input
edgeCases.description: Missing scheme, non-http(s) scheme, garbage text, or localhost/internal addresses entered in the form.
edgeCases.plain: A person can type a bad web address. The app must say no.
edgeCases.fixedNote: InputRules.UrlProblem: absolute http(s) URLs only; localhost, *.local, loopback, private, link-local (incl. 169.254.169.254) and unique-local IPv6 literals are refused (SSRF). Hostnames that resolve to private IPs are not caught (EC-031).

edgeCases.title: Duplicate URLs
edgeCases.description: The same URL added twice, including trailing-slash or case differences.
edgeCases.plain: The same address can be added two times.
edgeCases.fixedNote: POST /api/urls returns 409 when a live URL matches ignoring case and a trailing slash (Database.LiveUrlExistsAsync). Removed URLs do not count.

edgeCases.title: Time zones in the UI
edgeCases.description: Store UTC; display local time consistently.
edgeCases.plain: The server keeps one world time. The screen must show your local time.

edgeCases.title: TLS certificate errors
edgeCases.description: Expired or self-signed certificates — record as unhealthy with a clear reason vs. a generic failure.
edgeCases.plain: Some sites have a bad security certificate. We should show that reason.

edgeCases.title: Redirect loops
edgeCases.description: Too many redirects; also whether a 3xx counts as healthy.
edgeCases.plain: A site can send you to another address again and again.

edgeCases.title: Deleting a URL that has history
edgeCases.description: Decide whether results are removed with it or kept.
edgeCases.plain: If you remove an address, what happens to its old results?
edgeCases.fixedNote: Phase 2 task 3: DELETE /api/urls/{id} removes the URL and its check_results in one transaction (D-021). Superseded by D-023: remove is now a soft delete and history is kept.

edgeCases.title: Interval changed while a check is running
edgeCases.description: New interval should apply from the next due time without a restart.
edgeCases.plain: You change the time while a check runs. The new time must start on the next check.
edgeCases.fixedNote: Handled by design (URL-03, D-021): the scheduler reads interval_seconds from the database on every 5 s pass, so a new interval applies from the next tick without a restart.

edgeCases.title: SQLite write contention
edgeCases.description: Many parallel checks writing at once could hit 'database is locked'.
edgeCases.plain: Many writes at the same time can block the data file.

edgeCases.title: Huge response bodies
edgeCases.description: Avoid downloading large bodies; only headers are needed for status.
edgeCases.plain: Some pages are very big. We only need the first part of the answer.
edgeCases.fixedNote: Handled by design (D1-17): UrlChecker uses HttpCompletionOption.ResponseHeadersRead, so bodies are never downloaded.

edgeCases.title: Node or npm missing on the machine
edgeCases.description: The BuildWebUi MSBuild target runs npm on a fresh clone. If Node is not installed, the build fails with a raw npm error instead of a clear message. The README states that Node is required.
edgeCases.plain: The first run needs Node on the computer. If Node is missing, the error is hard to read.

edgeCases.title: Port 5080 already in use
edgeCases.description: If another program holds port 5080, the server fails to start. Nothing catches this or suggests another port.
edgeCases.plain: If another program uses the same door number, our app cannot start.

edgeCases.title: Stale server/wwwroot after a web/src change
edgeCases.description: BuildWebUi only runs npm run build when server/wwwroot/index.html is missing (D1-03). After editing web/src, the served UI stays old until npm --prefix web run build is run or wwwroot is deleted.
edgeCases.plain: If you change the web code, the old built page can still show. You must build again.

edgeCases.title: DNS error text depends on the operating system
edgeCases.description: A failed check stores the HttpRequestException message. On macOS it reads 'nodename nor servname provided, or not known'; on Windows and Linux it differs. The text is correct but not the same everywhere.
edgeCases.plain: The error words for a bad web address change from one computer type to another.

edgeCases.title: Unknown URL id on /api/urls/{id}/checks returns an empty list
edgeCases.description: The history route answers 200 with [] when the id does not exist, not 404. A client cannot tell 'no such URL' from 'no checks in this window'.
edgeCases.plain: If you ask for a URL that does not exist, you get an empty list, not a 'not found' error.

edgeCases.title: /api/urls/{id}/checks has no paging
edgeCases.description: A 7d call returns every check in the window (about 20,000 rows for a 30s URL). The UI does not poll this route, so it is acceptable for now.
edgeCases.plain: Asking for 7 days of one URL sends all of its checks at once. That can be a big reply.

edgeCases.title: Polling continues while the browser tab is hidden
edgeCases.description: The dashboard polls every 5 seconds even when nobody can see it. It wastes requests but does no harm on localhost.
edgeCases.plain: The page keeps asking for new data even when you are on another tab.

edgeCases.title: A slow poll can overlap the next one
edgeCases.description: If one request takes longer than 5 seconds, the next poll starts before it ends. The ignore flag only protects against a window change, so two replies for the same window could arrive out of order.
edgeCases.plain: If the server is slow, two requests can run at the same time. The older answer could show up last.

edgeCases.title: A fresh database makes the three windows look the same
edgeCases.description: With less than 1 hour of data, 1h, 24h, and 7d count the same checks. The picker seems to do nothing until history builds up. The README must say this.
edgeCases.plain: When the app is new, all three windows show the same numbers, because there is not enough history yet.

edgeCases.title: The summary query reads every row in the window on each poll
edgeCases.description: COUNT and AVG scan all rows of the URL in the window every 5 seconds. A 7d window is about 20,000 rows per 30s URL. A rollup table would fix this.
edgeCases.plain: The server counts thousands of rows again every 5 seconds. This is fast now, but it would slow down with a lot of history.

edgeCases.title: Some sites answer 403 to requests with no User-Agent
edgeCases.description: HttpClient sends no User-Agent by default. https://www.wikipedia.org answered 403 during testing, so it shows unhealthy although it is up. Fix: set a User-Agent on the named 'checker' client.
edgeCases.plain: Some websites refuse visitors that do not say who they are. Our checker does not say, so a working site can look broken.

edgeCases.title: A check still running when its URL is deleted saves an orphan result
edgeCases.description: Checks are not awaited by the loop (D-022). If the URL is deleted during its check, InsertCheckResultAsync still writes a row for the deleted url_id. SQLite foreign keys are not enforced by default, so nothing stops it. The row is never shown.
edgeCases.plain: If you delete a URL at the exact moment it is being checked, one hidden leftover row can be saved.
edgeCases.fixedNote: With soft delete (D-023) the urls row stays, so a late result still belongs to a real (removed) URL and shows on the All-checks page.

edgeCases.title: An add/re-time/remove error message disappears on the next successful poll
edgeCases.description: Mutation errors share the page error line with polling. The next good poll (up to 5 s later) clears it.
edgeCases.plain: If adding a URL fails, the error message shows for only a few seconds.

edgeCases.title: The interval box in a row does not follow a change made in another tab
edgeCases.description: IntervalEditor keeps its own state, set once from the first load.
edgeCases.plain: If you change an interval in a second browser tab, the first tab still shows the old number in the box.

edgeCases.title: Nothing is ever hard-deleted, so the database only grows
edgeCases.description: Retention archives instead of deleting (D-023) and removed URLs keep their rows. The archive table has no limit. A purge or export job would be needed for long-running use.
edgeCases.plain: We never throw data away, so the database file keeps getting bigger.

edgeCases.title: A removed URL cannot be restored from the UI
edgeCases.description: Soft delete sets deleted_at, but there is no undo button or endpoint. Re-adding the same URL creates a new id with empty history.
edgeCases.plain: If you remove a web address by mistake, you can add it again, but its old history stays under the old entry.

edgeCases.title: All-checks paging uses OFFSET, so pages shift when new results arrive
edgeCases.description: LIMIT/OFFSET paging over a growing table can repeat or skip a row between page clicks. Keyset paging (WHERE checked_at < last seen) would fix it. The page is not polled, which limits the effect.
edgeCases.plain: While you page through the history, new checks can push a row onto the next page twice.

edgeCases.title: Column widths and row heights are not saved
edgeCases.description: The CSS resize handles change the layout only until the page reloads. localStorage could keep them.
edgeCases.plain: If you resize a column and reload the page, it goes back to normal.

edgeCases.title: Retention days are not validated on the server
edgeCases.description: PUT /api/settings accepts 0 or negative days; 0 would archive every result on the next sweep (nothing is lost, it moves to the archive). The form uses min=1.
edgeCases.plain: The server does not stop a bad retention number, but the form in the page does.

edgeCases.title: A public hostname that resolves to a private IP passes the SSRF check
edgeCases.description: InputRules checks the host as written. A DNS name pointing at 10.x or 127.0.0.1 (or DNS rebinding) is not caught. A full fix resolves the name and checks every address at check time, inside a custom SocketsHttpHandler.ConnectCallback.
edgeCases.plain: Someone could use a normal-looking web name that secretly points inside our network. We only block addresses that are written out directly.

edgeCases.title: A manual check can overlap a scheduled check of the same URL
edgeCases.description: POST /api/urls/{id}/check does not use CheckScheduler's in-flight set, so if the scheduler starts the same URL at the same moment, two checks run and both rows are saved.
edgeCases.plain: If you press 'check now' at the exact moment the timer also checks, you get two results at once.

aiNotes.note: Claude recommended TypeScript for typed API calls. I rejected it for time and because I can defend plain JS faster. See D-003.
Claude flagged per-URL intervals as bonus scope and a risk to the 3-hour cap. I kept them in scope. See D-008.
Claude flagged that adding all four extras on top of three configurable intervals risks the 3-hour cap. Kept them, but moved them to a stretch tier built after the core. See D-012.

Skipped the Phase 1 discuss step. Claude picked the defaults for layout, data model, API, seeds, check behavior, and dashboard (D-014). These are AI decisions I accepted without debate; I review them during planning.

Claude generated all Phase 1 code from the locked plan (D1-01..D1-28). It built and ran without a rewrite, so there is no bad suggestion to report. Read these two files first to own the behavior: server/UrlChecker.cs (how one check is timed and classified) and server/CheckScheduler.cs (how due URLs are picked and saved). Database.cs follows the plan's warning about SQLite integers: Dapper fills a flat StatusRow class, and the records are built by hand. I did not test the shortcut, so I cannot say it would have failed.

Phase 1 code review (AI reviewer) found 3 items. Checked each by hand: npm install -> npm ci and the generic Node .gitignore were real. The DB-path warning was overstated: `dotnet run --project server` already uses server/ as working directory; only running the .dll directly from another folder put the DB elsewhere. Fixed all three anyway (the DB path is now pinned to the content root in Program.cs). Claude's own .csproj edit dropped a space and broke the XML; the fresh-clone rebuild caught it before commit.

Claude generated the Phase 2 window code from the plan (D-018, D-019). It built and passed the probe checks on the first run, so there is no bad suggestion to report. The plan warned about three pitfalls before the code was written: the DateTime-versus-text cutoff, the SQLite Int64 mapping (flat StatsRow and CheckRow classes), and a state name that hides the browser's window. I followed those warnings and did not test the unsafe versions. Read Database.GetWindowSummaryAsync first: it holds the aggregate, the 30-check strip query, and the cutoff handling.

Phase 2 task 2 (tests) was built inline by Claude in the main session instead of a planner + executor run, to save about 10 minutes. To show the tests are real, Claude broke the code on purpose twice (healthy rule <= 399 -> < 399; window filter returning everything) and saw exactly the guarding test fail each time, then reverted. All 12 passed on the first run, so no generated test needed a fix.

Phase 2 task 3 built inline. Mistake by Claude: the verify script ended with `lsof -ti tcp:5080 | xargs kill`. Port 5080 was already used by the owner's own running app, so the first curl checks hit the old build (405/404) and the cleanup killed the owner's process. Claude told the owner, and all later checks run on port 5081 and kill only the PID they started. Also found while testing: https://www.wikipedia.org answers 403 with no User-Agent (logged EC-022).

Task 4 was re-scoped by the owner (soft delete, no hard deletes, sorting, paging, colors, resizable table). Claude pointed out that 'never hard delete' conflicts with the brief's retention wording before building, and the owner picked archiving. Claude's first edit script broke on C# raw strings (""") inside a Python heredoc and left Program.cs half-updated; the build caught it, and Claude redid Database.cs from snippet files. API checks ran against a copy of the DB on port 5081 so the owner's running instance and data were not touched.

While checking pause/resume, Claude's first test sent the Content-Type header unquoted through a shell variable, so every PATCH looked like a 400; then a 404 turned out to be correct because the owner had removed URL 1 in their own instance. Both were test mistakes, not app bugs; the re-run on a live URL showed no checks while paused and a new check after resume.

The owner reported the dashboard table overflowing the screen. Claude had built the last UI rounds without looking at them. This time it ran the app on a DB copy and took headless Chrome screenshots at 1280/1440/1920 px, found the cause (a 240px one-line strip plus the full DNS error text), fixed it, and re-checked each width. A first fix still overflowed at 1280 px and needed a second pass. Lesson: screenshot UI changes before calling them done.

Two slips in the test round: the first npm test script (`node --test src/`) ran the folder as a file and failed; fixed with a glob. Then Claude's 'break it on purpose' check on logic.js used git checkout to restore, but the file was not committed yet, so the broken version stayed on disk; Claude noticed in the status output and restored it by hand before committing. All 7 frontend and 37 backend tests pass after.
